lesson.title: Straight Lines That Lie a Little: Sketching Bode Plots by Hand
lesson.summary: The asymptotic approximation replaces a curved Bode magnitude plot with straight line segments that are exact far from each corner frequency and at most 3 dB off right at it.
lesson.body:
A Bode magnitude plot shows how a transfer function's gain in decibels changes with frequency on a logarithmic frequency axis, and it is usually a smooth curve. Drawing that exact curve by hand is tedious, so engineers lean on the asymptotic approximation: replace the real curve with a handful of straight line segments, one for each region of the plot, that are exact far away from every corner frequency and only approximate near it.

For a single real pole, like the resistor capacitor low pass filter from earlier in this unit, the rule is simple. Below the corner frequency, the response is approximated as flat, 0 dB. Above the corner frequency, the response is approximated as a straight line falling at 20 dB per decade. The two lines meet exactly at the corner frequency itself, which is why that frequency is named for the geometric corner it creates on the plot.

The approximation is not exact anywhere except far from the corner, and the error is largest right at the corner. This is where the earlier chapters on half power point and corner frequency connect directly to this one: at the corner, the two asymptotic lines both sit at 0 dB, but the real curve sits at negative 3.01 dB, since the corner frequency is by definition the half power point. So the maximum error of the asymptotic approximation is exactly 3.01 dB, and it occurs exactly at the corner.

Move away from the corner and the error shrinks fast. At half the corner frequency, the real magnitude is 1 over the square root of 1 plus 0.5 squared, which is 1 over the square root of 1.25, or 0.8944, which is about negative 0.97 dB, while the flat asymptote still reads 0 dB, an error of about 1 dB. At twice the corner frequency, the real magnitude is 1 over the square root of 1 plus 2 squared, which is 1 over the square root of 5, or 0.4472, which is about negative 6.99 dB, while the sloped asymptote, having traveled 0.301 decades past the corner at negative 20 dB per decade, reads about negative 6.02 dB, again an error of about 1 dB. One full decade past the corner, using the same filter as the stopband chapter, the actual response was negative 20.04 dB against an asymptotic prediction of exactly negative 20 dB, an error of only 0.04 dB, essentially invisible on a hand sketch.

This pattern, about 3 dB of error at the corner, about 1 dB at a factor of 2 away, and under a tenth of a dB a decade away, is worth memorizing, because it tells you exactly how much to trust a hand drawn Bode plot and where to round the corner slightly if precision matters. It also generalizes cleanly: a circuit with several poles and zeros is sketched by adding up the slope contributions from each one at every corner frequency, a real pole contributing negative 20 dB per decade beyond its corner and a real zero contributing positive 20 dB per decade beyond its own, which is exactly the tool the next chapter needs once it introduces poles and zeros formally.
